Notes: Earliest documented Jewish residents (basis for Year Established): 2 Maccabees 12:8-9 says Judas Maccabee heard 'that the people of Jamnia planned in the same way to wipe out the Jews who lived among them' and attacked the Jamnians by night, setting fire to the harbor and fleet. Implies a Jewish minority living in a gentile (pagan/Phoenician-Hellenistic) town, c. 163 BCE (Judas's campaigns 164-163 BCE). No count. The earlier biblical notice that Uzziah of Judah breached Jabneh's walls (2 Chr 26:6, 8th c. BCE) records a conquest, not Judahite residence, so it is not used for Year Established. 2 Macc 12:40 also mentions amulets of the idols of Jamnia found on fallen Jewish soldiers.

Event: Varga & Betzer (IAA, 2025) state that in 163 BCE a battle at Yavne between the Seleucid army under Gorgias and the Jewish forces of Joseph ben Zechariah and Azariah ended in a Seleucid victory 'with 2,000 Jewish casualties' (1 Macc 5:55-62); they also note Gorgias used Yavne as a base after Emmaus (165 BCE). The 2,000 is a casualty count of a Judean army from outside the town, not residents; Population blank.

Event: Kletter & Ziffer (New Encyclopedia of Archaeological Excavations in the Holy Land) write that 'Simeon captured Gazara, Jaffa, and Jamnia (137 BC)' (Josephus, Ant. 13.215); Cendebaeus had earlier made Yavneh his base as governor of the coast. Jewish Virtual Library (EJ) prefers to attribute the capture to John Hyrcanus. No evidence of Jewish settlement at this date; Population blank.

Event: Hasmonean conquest. Varga & Betzer (IAA excavators) state 'In 122 BCE, John Hyrcanus captured Yavne, which remained in Hasmonean hands' until Pompey (citing Josephus Ant. 13.296; Kasher 1990). Their excavations show Hellenistic farmhouses at Yavne-East (areas Q, T2) established late 3rd c. BCE and 'likely continuing until the late second century BCE'. Before this, they note a 2nd c. BCE Delos dedication by men of Iamnia to Heracles and Hauronas (Phoenician/Hellenized pagan cult) and conflicts 'between local pagans and Jews'. No count.

Encyclopaedia Judaica (Jabneh) on Jewish Virtual Library: by the time of Alexander Jannaeus' siege of Ptolemais (c. 103 BCE) 'Jabneh was already a Hasmonean city (Jos., Ant., 13:324)' and 'the entire population was Jewish' (i.e. Judaized under the Hasmoneans). c. date inferred from the cited passage. Wholly Jewish town per the source but no figure given; Population blank.

Kletter & Ziffer: 'Alexander Jannaeus controlled Yavneh, from which point it is mentioned in ancient sources as a city with a Jewish population.' Year = midpoint of Jannaeus' reign (103-76 BCE), c. Presence of a Jewish urban population; no count. (Jewish Encyclopedia similarly says the Jews held it only from Jannaeus' time.)

Josephus, Antiquities 13.395 (Whiston): at the end of Alexander Jannaeus' reign (d. 76 BCE) 'the Jews were in possession of the following cities that had belonged to the Syrians, and Idumeans, and Phoenicians': 'At the sea-side, Strato's Tower, Apollonia, Joppa, Jamnia, Ashdod, Gaza...'. Jamnia under Jewish control; no population figure.

Event: Pompey's settlement (63 BCE). Josephus, Antiquities 14.75: Pompey 'restored' Marissa, Ashdod, Jamnia and Arethusa 'to their own inhabitants', i.e. detached Jamnia from the Hasmonean state as a non-Jewish town. EJ (JVL) describes this as an attempt to revive it as a gentile town, 'short-lived as an independent unit'. Sources do not say the Jews left; Population blank (not 0).

Event: Josephus, War 1.166: under Gabinius (c. 57 BCE) 'the following cities were restored;-Scythopolis, Samaria, Anthedon, Apollonia, Jamnia, Raphia...' 'while a great number of men readily ran to each of them, and became their inhabitants'. Resettlement of the town (ethnic identity of new settlers not stated). Date c. 57 BCE per Jewish Encyclopedia.

Strabo (Geography 16.2.28; Casaubon p. 759) as reported by the Jewish Encyclopedia: Jamnia 'was so populous that, with the surrounding villages, it could furnish 40,000 able warriors'. Ancient military-capacity figure for the town plus its villages (a regional figure, and its ethnic composition not stated); not a count of resident Jews. Population blank. Year c. 8 CE = approximate composition of Strabo's Geography (c. 7 BCE-23 CE); the figure may reflect earlier sources.

Philo, Legatio ad Gaium 200-202 (Yonge): 'There is a city called Jamnia; one of the most populous cities in all Judaea, which is inhabited by a promiscuous multitude, the greatest number of whom are Jews; but there are also some persons of other tribes from the neighbouring nations'. The gentile 'sojourners' erected a clay-brick altar to Gaius; the Jews pulled it down; the imperial revenue officer Capito reported it, provoking Gaius' order for his statue in the Temple. c. 39-40 CE. Jewish-majority mixed town; no figure.

Israel Antiquities Authority excavators (Betzer & Varga, 2021 press release): 'Toward the end of the Second Temple period, Yavne's mixed population had most Jewish residents.' The Yavne-East excavation found an industrial building dated 1st-3rd c. CE ('from the time of the Sanhedrin') whose floor held fragments of chalkstone 'measuring cups', 'identified with the Jewish population' (late Second Temple period and 2nd c. CE); the building is probably mostly post-70. Year 50 = 1st c. CE midpoint for 'end of the Second Temple period'. No count.

Encyclopaedia Judaica (JVL): 'By then, the city was purely Jewish and was a toparchy of Judea (Wars, 3:55)'. Josephus, War 3.56 lists Jamnia and Joppa as presiding over the neighbouring people among Judea's toparchies (description of c. 66 CE). Predominantly Jewish town per the source; no figure.

Event: Josephus, War 4.130: Vespasian marched 'from Caesarea to Jamnia and Azotus, and took them both; and when he had put garrisons into them', returning with many people who came over to him on his pledge of safety. Dated late 67 CE in Josephus' narrative (Wikipedia gives spring 68). No figure.

Event: Jewish Encyclopedia: 'owing to the turbulence of its large population, Vespasian twice found it necessary to besiege the city' (BJ 4.3.2; 4.8.1), implying a large, restive (Jewish) population during the revolt. No figure.

Event: Josephus, War 4.444 (68 CE): Vespasian 'passed on to Lydda and Jamnia; and when both these cities had come over to him', 'he placed a great many of those that had come over to him [from other places] as inhabitants therein'. Jamnia surrendered and was resettled with (presumably Jewish) deserters who had submitted to Rome; number not given.

Rabbinic tradition (Babylonian Talmud Gittin 56b; cited by EJ on JVL): during the siege of Jerusalem Johanan ben Zakkai asked Vespasian to 'give him Jabneh and its scholars'; after 70 his school functioned there as the Sanhedrin. Later tradition, not contemporary evidence; it presupposes a Jewish town receptive to the sages c. 69-70 CE. No figure.
